subject: Copywriting
title: Town Criers: The Human Billboard
description: A micro-lesson that makes Town Criers: The Human Billboard usable.

hook.text: Before newspapers, towns hired people to shout the news. Town criers were the first broadcast medium.

buildup.text: Criers announced royal decrees, market prices, and merchant offers. Their voice was the only ad channel.

discovery.text: The best criers used rhythm and rhyme. Catchy phrases stuck in minds—early jingles, spoken aloud.

twist.text: Criers were licensed by the king. Unauthorized shouting was illegal. Ad regulation started early.

climax.text: When the printing press arrived, criers faded. But their lesson survived: memorable beats forgettable.

punchline.text: The first ad men didn't write. They shouted.

quiz.question: What made town criers effective advertisers?

details.summary: Before mass literacy, town criers served as living advertisements — paid by merchants to announce goods, services, and public notices in marketplaces. Their verbal copy had to be memorable, rhythmic, and attention-grabbing. Town criers were the original copywriters, crafting persuasive messages...
details.whyItMatters: Town criers remind us that copywriting began as an oral tradition. The principle that copy must sound good when spoken aloud — tested by reading copy out loud — traces back to these earliest human billboards.
takeaways: Town criers were paid by merchants to announce products verbally
Their messages needed rhythm and memorability to cut through noise
Modern copywriting advice to 'read copy aloud' echoes this oral tradition

faq.question: How did town criers function as advertisers?
faq.answer: Merchants paid criers to walk through markets shouting announcements about goods and prices. Criers needed strong voices, memorable phrasing, and showmanship. They often used rhyme, repetition, and humor — the same tools used in modern jingles and slogans.

faq.question: When did town criers disappear?
faq.answer: Town criers declined as literacy increased and newspapers became common in the 17th-18th centuries. But the role never fully vanished — modern equivalents include radio DJs, podcast hosts, and influencers who use personality and voice to sell products.
